quotes.text: OAuth stands for open Authorization, and it's the standard that lets one app reach your data inside another app without ever holding your password.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: You might think OAuth is about signing you in, and it's actually about granting access, not proving identity.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Names the most common misconception about OAuth.

quotes.text: A password is your whole account forever and it can't be narrowed down. A token is limited to what you approved.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear contrast between passwords and scoped tokens.

quotes.text: Microsoft's own guidance keeps coming back to one rule called least privilege. Give the app the smallest permission that does the job.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Actionable permission-granting rule for Microsoft 365 apps.

quotes.text: Use the modern flow, add pkcs, match the redirect exactly and never treat a token as proof of identity.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Compact checklist of OAuth security best practices.

takeaways: OAuth 2.0 grants an app limited, temporary access through scoped tokens instead of sharing your password, but it does not prove identity.
The authorization code flow with PKCE is the modern default for user sign-in, while the implicit flow and password grant are deprecated.
In Microsoft 365, Microsoft Entra ID issues the tokens and Microsoft Graph accepts them, with delegated or application permissions granted by least privilege.
hook: Every time you click Sign in with Microsoft, OAuth 2.0 keeps your password out of the app. This episode explains the four players, the flows, tokens and scopes, and how it all works in Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Graph, for anyone who approves permission screens or builds apps. You will understand what you are really granting and which mistakes to avoid.
